items.title: 10.11 Electrode potentials (ease of oxidation and reduction)

blocks.text: During redox processes a redox equilibrium exists between two chemically related species in different oxidation states. When a metal is put into a solution of its ions, an electric potential (voltage) is established between the metal and the metal ions in solution; this is the electrode potential, and it indicates the ease of oxidation or reduction of a substance. When a copper rod is placed in an aqueous solution of its ions, the equilibrium Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s) exists, with two opposing reactions: metal atoms from the rod enter the solution as metal ions, leaving electrons behind on the surface of the electrode (Cu giving Cu2+ + 2e-), and ions in solution accept electrons from the rod and are deposited as metal atoms on its surface (Cu2+ + 2e- giving Cu). The redox equilibrium is established when the rate of electron gain equals the rate of electron loss.

For unreactive metals such as copper the equilibrium lies further to the right than for other metals: Cu2+ ions are relatively easy to reduce and gain electrons readily to form copper. For reactive metals such as vanadium the equilibrium V2+(aq) + 2e- giving V(s) lies further to the left: V2+ ions are relatively difficult to reduce and gain electrons much less readily. The position of equilibrium differs for different metals placed in solutions of their ions.

rows: difficult; V2+ gains electrons much less readily

blocks.prompt: Which of the two opposing surface reactions dominates for a reactive metal, and what sign of charge does the rod acquire?
blocks.explanation: For a reactive metal the atoms leave the rod as ions more readily than the ions return, so the dissolving reaction dominates until equilibrium; the electrons left behind give the rod a negative charge relative to the solution, and the more reactive the metal, the more negative its electrode potential.

items: Electrode potential: the voltage between a metal and its ions in solution, a measure of ease of oxidation or reduction; equilibrium M2+ + 2e- = M when electron gain and loss are equal.
Copper: equilibrium right, Cu2+ easy to reduce. Vanadium: equilibrium left, V2+ hard to reduce.
